title: r h
goal: Read and spell r, h; unlock "rat," "hat," "run" — and, since both letters are now taught, turn yesterday's two heart words ("are," "he") fully or partly decodable.
newToday: letters r, h (sounds /r/, /h/) — **one new sound per sitting**.
review: e, u; words cut, ten, sun.
heartLine: she, we (taught in the final combined sitting).
time: three sittings — A (~15 min), B (~15 min), C (~25–30 min).

A.text: Sam ran. Mom ran. The sun is hot. Is Sam hot? Is Mom hot? We are hot! She got a hat.

B.text: Dan ran to the dock. Nat ran to the dock. The sun got hot. Is Dan hot? Is Nat hot? We are hot. She got a mug.

questions: What got hot in the text?
Who got a hat, or a mug, at the end?
Think: what are some other ways people cool down on a very hot day at work or at play?

listen.title: The Morning Rotation
listen.passage: Before smartphones and ride-share apps existed, neighbors organized a shared morning school run with nothing more than a notebook taped inside someone's kitchen cabinet. Every family wrote down which mornings they could take the children, and everyone else simply trusted the schedule. It sounds old-fashioned, but the system worked because everyone had something to lose if they broke the trust — miss your turn, and you'd better believe your neighbors would remember. These days, apps handle the scheduling, but the core idea hasn't changed at all: a group of people agreeing to share both the effort and the waiting, so no single person carries the whole burden alone.

tier2.def: a plan that says when things will happen, especially times and dates.
tier2.full: a plan that says when things will happen, especially times and dates. "Check the bus schedule before you leave." "Our morning schedule is taped to the fridge." Your turn: what's on your schedule today?

tier2.def: something heavy or difficult that a person has to carry or deal with, not always a physical weight.
tier2.full: something heavy or difficult that a person has to carry or deal with, not always a physical weight. "Sharing the school run took some of the burden off Mom." "Debt can be a heavy burden." Your turn: what's one way people can share a burden?

questions: How did the old-fashioned rotation keep people honest, without any app?
What is the "core idea" the passage says hasn't changed, even with new technology?

warm.text: flash e, u. Read 3 review words: cut, ten, sun.

hear.text: /r/ — lips round slightly, tongue curls back without touching the roof of the mouth, like the start of "run."

meet.text: "This says /r/" (r). **Mouth cue:** /r/ is the first sound so far made with the tongue not touching anything — it just curls.
meet.mouthCue: /r/ is the first sound so far made with the tongue not touching anything — it just curls.

mini.text: r on sight 5/5; blend the 5 words above at ≥4/5.

warm.text: flash r. Read 3 review words: rat, ran, run.

hear.text: /h/ — just breath, no tongue or lip shaping at all, like a soft sigh, the start of "hat."

meet.text: "This says /h/" (h). **Mouth cue:** the first sound made with pure breath and nothing else — put a hand in front of the mouth and feel the puff of air with no buzz.
meet.mouthCue: the first sound made with pure breath and nothing else — put a hand in front of the mouth and feel the puff of air with no buzz.

mini.text: h on sight 5/5; blend the 5 words above at ≥4/5.

sittings.title: r, h together: heart words, Read it, Check (~25–30 min)

warm.text: flash r, h; blend 5 mixed words spanning both: rat, hop, hat, run, hen. Also re-read yesterday's two heart words ("are," "he") — point out that "he" is now fully decodable (h + e, both taught).

spell.text: 1. Segment and write: "run," "hat." 2. Sentence dictation: **"We ran and ran."** (We: heart word; ran: /r/ /a/ /n/; and: fully    decodable heart word.)

heart.note: "sh" is a two-letter spelling for one sound (a digraph) that isn't formally taught until Level 2, Lesson 2.1 — a little further ahead than most heart words reach back to. **Mark "sh" as heart for now**; the e is regular. Say: "'sh' is its own sound, a bit like c/k or ck were their own — you'll get the full lesson on it soon."
w isn't taught until **L1.11**. **Mark w as heart for now**; the e is regular. Like "he" was yesterday, this word will fully graduate off the heart-word list once w arrives.
